concerns.text: T016b (orchestration of sweeps) depends on T016a (sweep logic), but T016a depends on T016 (granularity logic). T016 is not marked [P] while T016a is. If T016 and T016a are distinct tasks modifying the same file `graph_construction.py`, they cannot run in parallel. The [P] tag on T016a is likely invalid if it implies parallel execution with T016.

T012 and T013 both depend on T009 and are marked [P]. However, both tasks describe implementing logic within the *same* file `graph_construction.py` (discretization module vs DAG construction logic). Implementing two distinct logic blocks in the same file simultaneously creates a merge conflict and shared state dependency, violating the [P] (parallel-safe) requirement.

T020, T021, T022, T023, T024 are all marked [P] (or implied parallel in the list) but all describe implementing logic within the *same* file `query_engine.py`. Parallel implementation of multiple features in a single file is not safe without strict file-splitting or interface-first contracts, which are not defined here.

T027 (baseline_runner.py) depends on T027a (acquire baseline). T027a is marked [P]. However, T027a is a setup/acquisition task (installing a container or cloning a repo) which is inherently sequential and stateful (requires disk space, network, environment setup). Marking it [P] suggests it can run in parallel with other foundational tasks (like T005 data loading), but if T027a fails or takes time, it blocks T027. More critically, if T027a is a 'local install', it may conflict with T002 (dependency init) if not ordered correctly. The [P] tag is misleading for an acquisition task that likely has hidden environmental dependencies.

T016 and T016a have nearly identical descriptions ('Implement parametric sweeping logic...'). T016a is marked [P] and depends on T016. This suggests a split of the same task into 'logic' and 'parallel logic', which is semantically confusing. The dependency chain T016 -> T016a -> T016b implies a serial flow, yet T016a is marked [P], creating a contradiction in the execution model.
